h1: Market research for a new beer brand: what to find out first
title: Market Research for a New Beer Brand | Craft Beer School
desc: What a new beer brand should find out before spending on brewing, packaging or launch, with the research method that answers each question.
teaser: Most new brands research the wrong thing first. Start with the decision you need to make, then pick the method.
standfirst: Market research is not a report you buy before launch. It is a short list of questions whose answers change what you brew, where you sell and what you charge. Here is the order we would answer them in.
sections: Start with the decision, not the topic

A founder who says "I want to research the market" usually has no decision in mind. Research that is not tied to a decision produces a deck and no action.

Write down the three or four choices that cost real money: which style leads the range, which pack size, which price, which city or channel first. Each one becomes a research question. If an answer would not change what you do, drop the question.

This is also how you keep the budget small. A focused study with one clear decision behind it beats a broad one that tries to describe everyone.
The four questions every new brand has to answer

1. Who will buy it? Not "all adults". A specific group in a specific place who already drink something you could replace.
  2. What are they drinking now? The shelf and the menu tell you. This is the job of a retail audit and of competitor research.
  3. What would they pay? Price is a research question as well as a costing one. See price research for a new drink.
  4. Will they like it? That is a tasting question, answered by a panel with blind samples and not by friends who want you to succeed.
Desk research first, because it is cheap

Before you ask anyone anything, read what exists. Trade association reports, state excise notices on permitted pack sizes and price bands, retailer websites and menus all show what is already sold and at what price. So do the brands' own social pages.

Treat any market size you find with suspicion unless it says how it was calculated. A number with no method behind it is decoration. If you need a size, build it yourself from the bottom up, as we describe in sizing a local beer market.
Then talk to people, in two different ways

Interviews and group discussions tell you why people choose what they choose. They are small, so they cannot tell you how many. Eight to twelve conversations with buyers, bar managers and retailers will usually surface the main reasons and the words customers use.

A survey tells you how many. It needs a sample large enough to trust and questions that do not lead the answer. Use interviews first to write better survey questions, then run the survey. Reversing the order is the common mistake.
A small plan a new brand can run

A plan that fits a modest budget: a week of desk research, a retail audit of twenty to thirty outlets in your launch area, ten interviews, one blind tasting with a panel of fifteen to twenty. Add a short survey if the decision needs numbers.

Keep a research log with the date, the method, the sample and what you decided as a result. When an investor or a partner asks why you chose a price or a style, the log is your answer.

One brewhouse point that research should respect: a recipe tested at 20 litres on a pilot kit can taste different at full scale, so run the panel on beer from the scale you will sell at where you can.

Good evidence has three marks. It comes from people who resemble your buyers. It records what they did and not only what they said. And you can say how you got it.

Weak evidence is easy to spot: a survey sent to your own followers, a tasting where everyone knew which beer was yours, a market size copied from a slide with no source. None of these is useless, but each should be labelled as a hint rather than a finding.

A useful habit is to write one line beside every finding: how strong is this? Strong means several methods agree. Weak means one conversation said so. Decisions that cost real money should rest on strong findings. Small, reversible bets can rest on weak ones.

Alcohol is a state subject in India, so the legal drinking age, permitted pack sizes, retail routes and pricing rules differ between states. A study done in one state cannot be assumed to hold in the next. If you plan to sell in more than one, research each as its own market.

For founders abroad, the same logic applies by country and region. Check local advertising rules too, because research that tests marketing messages must still respect them. Never recruit anyone under the legal age. Keep any tasting opt-in, with water on the table and no pressure to drink.

Brewers are good at the first and last step, the beer. The middle of the list, the sample design, the question wording and the arithmetic, is where small studies go wrong. That is the gap a research partner fills. Many founders find it only after a first attempt gives them a number they cannot defend.
faqs: How much does market research for a new beer brand cost?
It depends on the method and the sample, so we do not quote a figure in a guide. Desk research and a small audit cost your time. Surveys and panels cost more because recruiting people takes effort.
Can I just ask friends and family?
For early feedback on the idea, yes. For decisions about price or style, no. People who know you tend to be kind. They are rarely the people who will buy your beer off a shelf.
How many people do I need to survey?

It depends on how precise you need to be. As a rough guide, 400 random respondents gives a margin of about 5 percentage points on a simple yes or no question. Smaller groups are fine if you treat the result as direction only.
